captions.instagram:
How does a zip work?

Two rows of tiny teeth, each with a bump on top and a hollow underneath, and one slider with a wedge inside. See in slow motion how a zip locks tooth by tooth, why you cannot pull it apart sideways, and why a worn slider makes it split.

→ A zip is two rows of teeth, half a step out of line, and one slider.
→ Each tooth has a bump on top and a hollow underneath, stacked like cups.
→ Pull sideways and the tooth has no room to climb over the bump. Locked.
→ Inside the slider, each tape bends, and the bend fans its teeth apart.
→ Each head tips into the open gap across the way, one tooth at a time.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/zipclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a zip work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Two rows of tiny teeth, each with a bump on top and a hollow underneath, and one slider with a wedge inside. See in slow motion how a zip locks tooth by tooth, why you cannot pull it apart sideways, and why a worn slider makes it split.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/zipclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/zipclear

In this video:
• Two tapes, two rows of teeth, one slider. A zip is two cloth tapes, each with a row of small teeth clamped along a corded edge.
• A bump on top, a hollow underneath. Each tooth head has a small bump on top and a matching hollow below.
• The slider bends the tape. Inside the slider is a Y-shaped channel.
• A wedge, working on one tooth at a time. Going down, the diamond in the fork of the Y is a wedge driven between the rows.
• Why a zip splits behind the slider. A slider is cast from soft zinc alloy.
• Metal, moulded plastic and coil. Metal teeth are stamped and clamped on.

Glassbox opens one box a day: an interactive model of how something works, plus the code behind it.
